title: Appendix A: Recovery Instrumentation and Auditing
html:
Appendix A: Recovery Instrumentation and Auditing

Several chapters distinguish a successful request from a completed operation. A caller can receive a timeout after an external operation succeeds. A consumer can acknowledge a message after recording work that another process still needs to perform. A recovery worker can execute repeatedly without establishing the result it was assigned to investigate.

Engineers operating these mechanisms need evidence about unfinished work. They need to know which operations require action, how old those operations are, whether recovery attempts are making progress, and whether records in different components agree.

This appendix uses Baodium’s recovery tasks to make those measurements concrete. The same questions apply to document processing, account provisioning, reservation systems, external API integrations, and other applications in which accepting work and completing its effect are separate events.

Recovery Measurements

Queue depth does not describe the experience of every operation in the queue. Ten recently created tasks may complete during the next recovery pass. One task that has failed on every attempt for several hours can require investigation even when the queue contains nothing else.

For each recovery category, the operational view includes four related measurements.

Outstanding work.

The number of distinct operations or tasks requiring action. Repeated attempts at one task do not create additional business operations in this count.

Oldest unresolved age.

The elapsed time since the oldest outstanding obligation arose. Reclaiming a task or scheduling another attempt preserves that starting timestamp.

Arrival and resolution rates.

The rate at which work enters the category and the rate at which it leaves with a recorded outcome. Transfers to another recovery category are reported separately from business resolution.

Attempt outcomes.

The results of recovery attempts, including established outcomes, inconclusive observations, transient failures, and cases requiring review.

Each category needs a defined starting event and completion rule. For an outbox event, age begins at the business commit that created the publication obligation. For a compensation task, it begins when the application records that compensation is required.

Transferring a task to manual review preserves the original unresolved timestamp and records when review began. Otherwise, repeated transfers between queues could make an old obligation appear recent.

Measurement Collection

The following example updates exporter measurements from one repository snapshot. The repository returns every configured recovery category, including categories with no outstanding work. An empty category has a count of zero and an oldest age of zero.

If collection fails, the exporter records the failure and does not replace the previous business measurements with zeros. The observation timestamp allows an alert evaluator to determine whether those previous measurements are too old to use.

def publish_recovery_snapshot():
    try:
        snapshot = recovery_repo.snapshot()
    except RecoveryReadError:
        metrics.increment(
            "recovery.snapshot.read_failures"
        )
        return

    for category in snapshot.categories:
        labels = {
            "category": category.name,
            "region": snapshot.region,
        }
        metrics.gauge(
            "recovery.outstanding",
            category.outstanding_count,
            labels=labels,
        )
        metrics.gauge(
            "recovery.oldest_seconds",
            category.oldest_age_seconds,
            labels=labels,
        )

    metrics.gauge(
        "recovery.snapshot.observed_at_seconds",
        snapshot.observed_at.timestamp(),
        labels={"region": snapshot.region},
    )

The repository calculates counts and ages from the same database snapshot where practical. It uses the database observation time to calculate age, avoiding subtraction of timestamps from unrelated host clocks. Collection queries need appropriate indexes and bounded work because the exporter may run while the recovery backlog is large.

The final timestamp identifies the observation time of the last snapshot whose local metric updates completed; these calls cannot confirm that a monitoring backend received every value. Delivery follows the metric client’s export mechanism.

Sequential gauge updates also do not make the collection atomic; a scrape can occur between updates and observe values from two snapshots. If an alert compares categories or relies on a consistent relationship between several measurements, the exporter can build an immutable snapshot and replace the published reference under synchronization. The collector then reads that reference once for each collection.

The alert evaluator checks observation age before interpreting business measurements. Comparing a database timestamp with the evaluator’s clock also requires accounting for clock skew. Separate monitoring detects export failures, an unavailable exporter, and absent series, because an exporter that has stopped cannot report its own collection failure.

Region and recovery category are bounded metric labels, while individual operation identifiers belong in access-controlled records and diagnostic events. Using an operation identifier as a metric label would create a separate time series for each operation.

Arrival, resolution, and attempt rates can be calculated from committed transition records or exported as counters. A counter emitted outside the business transaction can lose an increment or repeat it after a failure. Exact accounting therefore requires durable transition records or another collection method that accounts for restarts and duplicate export. Approximate counters can support diagnosis when their limitations are understood.

Operation Evidence

An engineer investigating an unresolved operation needs to reconstruct what the application attempted and what it learned afterward. The durable record identifies the business operation, its request parameters or fingerprint, its current state, and the version used for conditional updates.

Where an external service is involved, the record also identifies the external account or tenant, operation type, idempotency identity, and any external operation identifier obtained. Attempt records distinguish dispatch intent, observed responses, and later status lookups.

A dispatch-intent record precedes the network call, so recovery still needs to determine whether the external service received it. After a timeout, the operation may have succeeded. Preserve the intent, attempt, and later evidence so another worker can investigate after the original process terminates.

The record also identifies when the obligation arose, when it was last examined, and which action is permitted next. A missing external identifier must not exclude an operation from recovery if the original request may have reached the dependency.

Retention follows the application’s recovery, replay, and audit requirements. Expiring a cached response does not, by itself, justify deleting the operation history needed to interpret a later retry.

Independent Audits

Recovery processes investigate work already known to require attention. An independent audit can discover disagreements outside that population, including an operation that the application incorrectly recorded as complete.

The comparison needs coverage in both directions. Starting from local records, the auditor checks the corresponding external results. Starting from an external inventory or report, it checks that each relevant result has a corresponding local operation.

For example, an export service can compare completed export records with objects in destination storage. Looking up only the object names recorded locally can identify missing exports, but it cannot discover every untracked object. Enumerating the destination provides the other direction of the comparison.

The same distinction applies to Baodium’s payment example. Looking up provider identifiers stored in the application can investigate known operations. Discovering an unmatched provider-side effect requires provider records that cover the relevant account and interval.

An audit records:

  • The account, tenant, region, or other scope being compared.

  • The stable identifiers used to match records.

  • The interval, report, or source cursor covered by the run.

  • The observation time and whether the source considers that interval complete.

  • The fields and outcome mappings used to identify disagreement.

Raw status strings are rarely a sufficient comparison contract, because components may describe different stages of the same operation. Successful publication of an event and completion of the consumer’s business effect, for instance, are distinct outcomes.

Reports may become available after the events they describe. Overlapping scans and deduplication allow an auditor to revisit an interval when late records are possible. An incomplete report is no evidence that an operation is absent.

The audit distinguishes an unmatched local record, an unmatched external result, conflicting business details, and a conflicting outcome. Temporary lookup failures are recorded as unavailable evidence rather than converted into business failures.

An audit batch advances its checkpoint after its observations and review cases have been committed durably. Repeating the batch must not create another open case for the same discrepancy. If a resolved operation develops a new discrepancy, the application reopens the case or records a linked occurrence under an explicit rule.

Applying Recovery Evidence

A recovery worker associates each observation with the operation it describes. Before applying the observation, it also needs to account for concurrent changes to the local records.

Suppose a worker establishes that an external operation succeeded after the caller received a pending response. Another worker or customer action may have changed the local record in the meantime. The update therefore checks the original operation identity, expected version, and permitted transition.

Related local changes commit atomically. If a conditional update affects no rows, the worker rereads the records before deciding what to do next, and it cannot assume that another worker applied the same result.

An established external success does not authorize every subsequent business action. If the customer canceled the original request, the application may need compensation or review. The external fact and the current business decision both need to be recorded.

Absence requires a separate check. A response such as NOT_FOUND establishes failure only when the lookup has the required scope and authority, and the dependency’s contract establishes that an earlier in-flight request cannot subsequently complete.

Without that guarantee, the outcome is unresolved. Further lookup, a retry under the original identity, or manual review depends on the dependency’s documented behavior and retention period.

These are the identity and guarded-transition requirements developed in Chapter 3. The consumer-side transaction and replay requirements in Chapter 12 apply when recovery work is delivered through messages. Instrumentation and auditing provide evidence for those mechanisms without replacing their correctness checks.

Alerts and Operator Actions

A useful recovery alert connects a measurement to an investigation or action an owner can perform. Increasing unresolved age can indicate failed dependency access, repeated inconclusive lookups, or a task that workers cannot complete. An increasing manual-review backlog may require additional reviewers or a change to admission policy.

Thresholds depend on customer commitments, retention limits, and the rate at which recovery workers can resolve work. A task approaching the end of an external idempotency or lookup period may require attention before a depth-based alert fires.

The operational view provides collection time, depth, oldest age, recent resolution rate, and the responsible owner. From the alert, the engineer needs access to the affected records and the evidence required to determine their next permitted action.
